cards.raw_front: In system identification (Chapter 2 & Section 5.1), what is the fundamental definition of a **linear system** (including time-varying linear systems)?
cards.raw_back: A system is **linear** if a linear combination of inputs leads to the **same linear combination of the corresponding outputs** (principle of superposition), even if the impulse response weights change with time $t$.

cards.anki_back: A system is linear if a linear combination of inputs leads to the same linear combination of the corresponding outputs (principle of superposition), even if the impulse response weights change with time \(t\).

cards.raw_front:
In terms of the time-indexed lag impulse response $g_t(k)$, a general discrete-time linear time-varying (LTV) system is described by Eq. (5.1):
$$y(t) = {{c1::\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} g_t(k)u(t-k) + v(t)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Here $k \ge 1$ is the elapsed lag since the input was applied at time $t-k$, and subscript $t$ indicates that the impulse response sequence changes with the observation time $t$.
cards.anki_front:
In terms of the time-indexed lag impulse response \(g_t(k)\), a general discrete-time linear time-varying (LTV) system is described by Eq. (5.1):

\(y(t) =\) {{c1::\(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} g_t(k)u(t-k) + v(t)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(k \ge 1\) is the elapsed lag since the input was applied at time \(t-k\), and subscript \(t\) indicates that the impulse response sequence changes with the observation time \(t\).

cards.raw_front:
In linear time-varying (LTV) models, how is the lag-indexed impulse response $g_t(k)$ related to the two-argument **weighting function** $\tilde{g}(t, s)$?
$${{c1::g_t(k) = \tilde{g}(t, t-k)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Equivalently, setting $s = t - k$ (so $k = t - s$), $\tilde{g}(t, s) = g_t(t - s)$.
cards.anki_front:
In linear time-varying (LTV) models, how is the lag-indexed impulse response \(g_t(k)\) related to the two-argument weighting function \(\tilde{g}(t, s)\)?
{{c1::\(g_t(k) = \tilde{g}(t, t-k)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Equivalently, setting \(s = t - k\) (so \(k = t - s\)), \(\tilde{g}(t, s) = g_t(t - s)\).

cards.raw_front: **Notation Trap**: Contrast the meanings of the arguments in $g_t(k)$ versus $\tilde{g}(t, s)$ for a linear time-varying system.
cards.raw_back:
- **$g_t(k)$**: Indexed by output observation time $t$ and **relative lag** $k = t - s \ge 1$ (elapsed steps since the input occurred at $t-k$).
- **$\tilde{g}(t, s)$**: Indexed by absolute output observation time $t$ and **absolute input application time** $s \le t - 1$.
cards.anki_front: Notation Trap: Contrast the meanings of the arguments in \(g_t(k)\) versus \(\tilde{g}(t, s)\) for a linear time-varying system.
cards.anki_back:
- \(g_t(k)\): Indexed by output observation time \(t\) and relative lag \(k = t - s \ge 1\) (elapsed steps since the input occurred at \(t-k\)).
- \(\tilde{g}(t, s)\): Indexed by absolute output observation time \(t\) and absolute input application time \(s \le t - 1\).

cards.raw_front: What is the physical definition of the **weighting function** $\tilde{g}(t, s)$ ($t = s, s+1, \dots$), and why is it called that?
cards.raw_back:
$\tilde{g}(t, s)$ is the **response at time $t$ to a unit input pulse applied at time $s$**.

It is called the *weighting function* because in the convolution sum $y(t) = \sum_{s=-\infty}^{t-1} \tilde{g}(t, s)u(s) + v(t)$, it describes the **weight** that the input applied at time $s$ has in forming the output at time $t$.
cards.anki_front: What is the physical definition of the weighting function \(\tilde{g}(t, s)\) (\(t = s, s+1, \dots\)), and why is it called that?
cards.anki_back:
\(\tilde{g}(t, s)\) is the response at time \(t\) to a unit input pulse applied at time \(s\).

It is called the weighting function because in the convolution sum \(y(t) = \sum_{s=-\infty}^{t-1} \tilde{g}(t, s)u(s) + v(t)\), it describes the weight that the input applied at time \(s\) has in forming the output at time \(t\).

cards.raw_front:
Expressed in terms of the two-argument weighting function $\tilde{g}(t, s)$, the input-output relationship of a general linear time-varying (LTV) system is given by Eq. (5.2):
$$y(t) = {{c1::\sum_{s=-\infty}^{t-1} \tilde{g}(t, s)u(s) + v(t)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Obtained from $y(t) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty g_t(k)u(t-k) + v(t)$ via the substitution $s = t - k$ and $g_t(k) = \tilde{g}(t, t-k) = \tilde{g}(t, s)$.
cards.anki_front:
Expressed in terms of the two-argument weighting function \(\tilde{g}(t, s)\), the input-output relationship of a general linear time-varying (LTV) system is given by Eq. (5.2):

\(y(t) =\) {{c1::\(\sum_{s=-\infty}^{t-1} \tilde{g}(t, s)u(s) + v(t)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Obtained from \(y(t) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty g_t(k)u(t-k) + v(t)\) via the substitution \(s = t - k\) and \(g_t(k) = \tilde{g}(t, t-k) = \tilde{g}(t, s)\).

cards.raw_front: In Eq. (5.2), $y(t) = \sum_{s={{c1::-\infty}}}^{{{c1::t-1}}} \tilde{g}(t, s)u(s) + v(t)$, what are the lower and upper limits of the summation over absolute input time $s$, and why?
cards.raw_back: The summation runs from $s = -\infty$ to $s = t - 1$ because $k = t - s$ runs from $k = 1$ (strictly causal one-step delay) to $k = \infty$.
cards.anki_front: In Eq. (5.2), \(y(t) = \sum_{s=\) {{c1::\(-\infty\)}} \(}^{\) {{c1::\(t-1\)}} \(} \tilde{g}(t, s)u(s) + v(t)\), what are the lower and upper limits of the summation over absolute input time \(s\), and why?
cards.anki_back: The summation runs from \(s = -\infty\) to \(s = t - 1\) because \(k = t - s\) runs from \(k = 1\) (strictly causal one-step delay) to \(k = \infty\).

cards.raw_front:
How is the **time-varying transfer function** (or transfer operator) $G_t(q)$ formally defined in Eq. (5.3)?
$$G_t(q) = {{c1::\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} g_t(k)q^{-k}}}$$
cards.raw_back: Here $q^{-1}$ is the backward shift operator ($q^{-k}u(t) = u(t-k)$), so $y(t) = G_t(q)u(t) + v(t)$.
cards.anki_front:
How is the time-varying transfer function (or transfer operator) \(G_t(q)\) formally defined in Eq. (5.3)?

\(G_t(q) =\) {{c1::\(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} g_t(k)q^{-k} \)}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(q^{-1} \) is the backward shift operator (\(q^{-k}u(t) = u(t-k)\)), so \(y(t) = G_t(q)u(t) + v(t)\).

cards.raw_front: Although one can define a time-varying transfer operator $G_t(q) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty g_t(k)q^{-k}$, how are linear time-varying (LTV) models almost always formulated in practice?
cards.raw_back: In practice, it is much easier to formulate and deal with time variation using **time-varying state-space models** rather than time-varying transfer functions.
cards.anki_front: Although one can define a time-varying transfer operator \(G_t(q) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty g_t(k)q^{-k} \), how are linear time-varying (LTV) models almost always formulated in practice?
cards.anki_back: In practice, it is much easier to formulate and deal with time variation using time-varying state-space models rather than time-varying transfer functions.

cards.raw_front:
In innovations form, a parameterized **linear time-varying (LTV) state-space model** is given by Eq. (5.4):
$$x(t+1, \theta) = {{c1::A_t(\theta)x(t, \theta) + B_t(\theta)u(t) + K_t(\theta)e(t)}}$$
$$y(t) = {{c1::C_t(\theta)x(t, \theta) + e(t)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Obtained directly from the LTI innovations state-space model (4.91) by allowing the system matrices $A_t(\theta), B_t(\theta), C_t(\theta), K_t(\theta)$ to depend explicitly on time $t$.
cards.anki_front:
In innovations form, a parameterized linear time-varying (LTV) state-space model is given by Eq. (5.4):

\(x(t+1, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(A_t(\theta)x(t, \theta) + B_t(\theta)u(t) + K_t(\theta)e(t)\)}}

\(y(t) =\) {{c1::\(C_t(\theta)x(t, \theta) + e(t)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Obtained directly from the LTI innovations state-space model (4.91) by allowing the system matrices \(A_t(\theta), B_t(\theta), C_t(\theta), K_t(\theta)\) to depend explicitly on time \(t\).

cards.raw_front:
For the LTV innovations state-space model (5.4), the **one-step-ahead predictor** state update and output equations in Eq. (5.5) are:
$$\hat{x}(t+1, \theta) = {{c1::[A_t(\theta) - K_t(\theta)C_t(\theta)]\hat{x}(t, \theta) + B_t(\theta)u(t) + K_t(\theta)y(t)}}$$
$$\hat{y}(t|\theta) = {{c1::C_t(\theta)\hat{x}(t, \theta)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Derived by substituting the innovation $e(t) = y(t) - C_t(\theta)\hat{x}(t, \theta)$ into the state update equation.
cards.anki_front:
For the LTV innovations state-space model (5.4), the one-step-ahead predictor state update and output equations in Eq. (5.5) are:

\(\hat{x}(t+1, \theta) =\) {{c1::\([A_t(\theta) - K_t(\theta)C_t(\theta)]\hat{x}(t, \theta) + B_t(\theta)u(t) + K_t(\theta)y(t)\)}}

\(\hat{y}(t|\theta) =\) {{c1::\(C_t(\theta)\hat{x}(t, \theta)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Derived by substituting the innovation \(e(t) = y(t) - C_t(\theta)\hat{x}(t, \theta)\) into the state update equation.

cards.raw_front:
When unrolled into an infinite-history input-output expansion, the LTV predictor $\hat{y}(t|\theta)$ of Eq. (5.5) takes the form of Eq. (5.6):
$$\hat{y}(t|\theta) = {{c1::\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_t^u(k, \theta)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_t^y(k, \theta)y(t-k)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Here $w_t^u(k, \theta)$ and $w_t^y(k, \theta)$ are the time-varying predictor impulse response weights for past inputs $u(t-k)$ and past outputs $y(t-k)$.
cards.anki_front:
When unrolled into an infinite-history input-output expansion, the LTV predictor \(\hat{y}(t|\theta)\) of Eq. (5.5) takes the form of Eq. (5.6):

\(\hat{y}(t|\theta) =\) {{c1::\(\sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_t^u(k, \theta)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^{\infty} w_t^y(k, \theta)y(t-k)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(w_t^u(k, \theta)\) and \(w_t^y(k, \theta)\) are the time-varying predictor impulse response weights for past inputs \(u(t-k)\) and past outputs \(y(t-k)\).

cards.raw_front:
In the LTV predictor expansion $\hat{y}(t|\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^u(k, \theta)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^y(k, \theta)y(t-k)$, the **input predictor weight** $w_t^u(k, \theta)$ is given by Eq. (5.7a):
$$w_t^u(k, \theta) = {{c1::C_t(\theta) \prod_{j=t-k+1}^{t-1} [A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)] B_{t-k}(\theta)}}$$
cards.raw_back: (Note: Ljung writes the product index as $\prod_{j=t-k}^{t-1}$; an input $u(t-k)$ enters via $B_{t-k}(\theta)$ at step $t-k+1$, is propagated by the closed-loop observer matrices $[A_j - K_j C_j]$ up to $t-1$, and is read out by $C_t(\theta)$ at time $t$.)
cards.anki_front:
In the LTV predictor expansion \(\hat{y}(t|\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^u(k, \theta)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^y(k, \theta)y(t-k)\), the input predictor weight \(w_t^u(k, \theta)\) is given by Eq. (5.7a):

\(w_t^u(k, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(C_t(\theta) \prod_{j=t-k+1}^{t-1} [A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)] B_{t-k}(\theta)\)}}
cards.anki_back: (Note: Ljung writes the product index as \(\prod_{j=t-k}^{t-1} \); an input \(u(t-k)\) enters via \(B_{t-k}(\theta)\) at step \(t-k+1\), is propagated by the closed-loop observer matrices \([A_j - K_j C_j]\) up to \(t-1\), and is read out by \(C_t(\theta)\) at time \(t\).)

cards.raw_front:
In the LTV predictor expansion $\hat{y}(t|\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^u(k, \theta)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^y(k, \theta)y(t-k)$, the **output predictor weight** $w_t^y(k, \theta)$ is given by Eq. (5.7b):
$$w_t^y(k, \theta) = {{c1::C_t(\theta) \prod_{j=t-k+1}^{t-1} [A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)] K_{t-k}(\theta)}}$$
cards.raw_back: (Written in Ljung Eq. 5.7 with product bounds $\prod_{j=t-k}^{t-1}$.) Past output $y(t-k)$ enters via the Kalman gain $K_{t-k}(\theta)$, propagates through the time-varying observer transition matrices $[A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)]$, and is mapped to the output at time $t$ via $C_t(\theta)$.
cards.anki_front:
In the LTV predictor expansion \(\hat{y}(t|\theta) = \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^u(k, \theta)u(t-k) + \sum_{k=1}^\infty w_t^y(k, \theta)y(t-k)\), the output predictor weight \(w_t^y(k, \theta)\) is given by Eq. (5.7b):

\(w_t^y(k, \theta) =\) {{c1::\(C_t(\theta) \prod_{j=t-k+1}^{t-1} [A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)] K_{t-k}(\theta)\)}}
cards.anki_back: (Written in Ljung Eq. 5.7 with product bounds \(\prod_{j=t-k}^{t-1} \).) Past output \(y(t-k)\) enters via the Kalman gain \(K_{t-k}(\theta)\), propagates through the time-varying observer transition matrices \([A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)]\), and is mapped to the output at time \(t\) via \(C_t(\theta)\).

cards.raw_front: In Eq. (5.7), why must the transition product $\prod [A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)]$ cannot be simplified to a matrix power $[A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)]^{k-1}$, and why does the multiplication order matter?
cards.raw_back: Because the observer matrices $\tilde{A}_j(\theta) = A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)$ vary with time index $j$, and **matrix multiplication is non-commutative** ($\tilde{A}_{t-1}\tilde{A}_{t-2} \ne \tilde{A}_{t-2}\tilde{A}_{t-1}$). The matrices must be left-multiplied in chronological order from $t-k$ up to $t-1$.
cards.anki_front: In Eq. (5.7), why must the transition product \(\prod [A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)]\) cannot be simplified to a matrix power \([A(\theta) - K(\theta)C(\theta)]^{k-1} \), and why does the multiplication order matter?
cards.anki_back: Because the observer matrices \(\tilde{A}_j(\theta) = A_j(\theta) - K_j(\theta)C_j(\theta)\) vary with time index \(j\), and matrix multiplication is non-commutative (\(\tilde{A}_{t-1}\tilde{A}_{t-2} \ne \tilde{A}_{t-2}\tilde{A}_{t-1} \)). The matrices must be left-multiplied in chronological order from \(t-k\) up to \(t-1\).

cards.raw_front: How is the one-step-ahead predictor obtained if an LTV state-space model is specified interms of process/measurement noise covariances $A_t, B_t, C_t, R_1(t), R_{12}(t), R_2(t)$ (as in Eqs. 4.84–4.85) instead of directly parameterizing $K_t(\theta)$?
cards.raw_back: The time-varying predictor is still given by the **Kalman filter equations (4.94)–(4.95)**, where the Riccati equation and Kalman gain $K(t, \theta)$ are recursively updated at each step $t$ using the time-varying system and covariance matrices $A_t, B_t, C_t, R_1(t), R_{12}(t), R_2(t)$.
cards.anki_front: How is the one-step-ahead predictor obtained if an LTV state-space model is specified interms of process/measurement noise covariances \(A_t, B_t, C_t, R_1(t), R_{12}(t), R_2(t)\) (as in Eqs. 4.84–4.85) instead of directly parameterizing \(K_t(\theta)\)?
cards.anki_back: The time-varying predictor is still given by the Kalman filter equations (4.94)–(4.95), where the Riccati equation and Kalman gain \(K(t, \theta)\) are recursively updated at each step \(t\) using the time-varying system and covariance matrices \(A_t, B_t, C_t, R_1(t), R_{12}(t), R_2(t)\).

cards.raw_front: What are the **two most common practical situations** where a physically time-invariant or nonlinear system leads to a **linear time-varying (LTV)** discrete-time model?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Non-equal (non-uniform) sampling intervals** (including multirate sampling and missing output data) applied to a continuous-time LTI system.
2. **Linearization of a nonlinear system** around a time-varying nominal trajectory $(u^*(t), x^*(t))$.
cards.anki_front: What are the two most common practical situations where a physically time-invariant or nonlinear system leads to a linear time-varying (LTV) discrete-time model?
cards.anki_back:
1. Non-equal (non-uniform) sampling intervals (including multirate sampling and missing output data) applied to a continuous-time LTI system.
2. Linearization of a nonlinear system around a time-varying nominal trajectory \((u^*(t), x^*(t))\).

cards.raw_front: Why does sampling a continuous-time **linear time-invariant (LTI)** system at non-equal time instants $t = t_k$ ($k = 1, 2, \dots$) yield a **time-varying** discrete-time state-space model?
cards.raw_back:
Discretizing from $t_k$ to $t_{k+1}$ using the exact zero-order-hold sampling formulas (4.66)–(4.68) depends on the sampling interval $T_k = t_{k+1} - t_k$:
$$F_k = e^{AT_k}, \quad G_k = \int_0^{T_k} e^{As}B\,ds$$
When $T_k$ is not constant, the discrete-time matrices $F(T_k)$ and $G(T_k)$ change from step $k$ to step $k+1$, producing a linear time-varying (LTV) model.
cards.anki_front: Why does sampling a continuous-time linear time-invariant (LTI) system at non-equal time instants \(t = t_k\) (\(k = 1, 2, \dots\)) yield a time-varying discrete-time state-space model?
cards.anki_back:
Discretizing from \(t_k\) to \(t_{k+1} \) using the exact zero-order-hold sampling formulas (4.66)–(4.68) depends on the sampling interval \(T_k = t_{k+1} - t_k\):
\[F_k = e^{AT_k}, \quad G_k = \int_0^{T_k} e^{As}B\,ds\]
When \(T_k\) is not constant, the discrete-time matrices \(F(T_k)\) and \(G(T_k)\) change from step \(k\) to step \(k+1\), producing a linear time-varying (LTV) model.

cards.raw_front: How are **multirate systems** (where different output variables are sampled at different rates) and **missing output data** represented within the LTV state-space framework (5.4)?
cards.raw_back: They are modeled by making the **output matrix $C_t(\theta)$ time-varying** so that at each time instant $t$, $C_t(\theta)$ picks out (or masks) only the specific state/output channels that are actually sampled and available at instant $t$ (see also Section 14.2).
cards.anki_front: How are multirate systems (where different output variables are sampled at different rates) and missing output data represented within the LTV state-space framework (5.4)?
cards.anki_back: They are modeled by making the output matrix \(C_t(\theta)\) time-varying so that at each time instant \(t\), \(C_t(\theta)\) picks out (or masks) only the specific state/output channels that are actually sampled and available at instant \(t\) (see also Section 14.2).

cards.raw_front:
Prior to linearization, the general discrete-time **nonlinear state-space system** with multiplicative/state-dependent disturbance gains is written in Eq. (5.8) as:
$$x(t+1) = {{c1::f(x(t), u(t)) + r(x(t), u(t))w(t)}}$$
$$y(t) = {{c1::h(x(t)) + m(x(t), u(t))v(t)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Here $f(\cdot, \cdot)$ and $h(\cdot)$ are nonlinear state transition and output functions, and $r(\cdot, \cdot), m(\cdot, \cdot)$ weight the process noise $w(t)$ and measurement noise $v(t)$.
cards.anki_front:
Prior to linearization, the general discrete-time nonlinear state-space system with multiplicative/state-dependent disturbance gains is written in Eq. (5.8) as:

\(x(t+1) =\) {{c1::\(f(x(t), u(t)) + r(x(t), u(t))w(t)\)}}

\(y(t) =\) {{c1::\(h(x(t)) + m(x(t), u(t))v(t)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(f(\cdot, \cdot)\) and \(h(\cdot)\) are nonlinear state transition and output functions, and \(r(\cdot, \cdot), m(\cdot, \cdot)\) weight the process noise \(w(t)\) and measurement noise \(v(t)\).

cards.raw_front: What two assumptions are made on the disturbances $\{w(t)\}$ and $\{v(t)\}$ and on the nominal trajectory $(u^*(t), x^*(t))$ when linearizing the nonlinear system (5.8)?
cards.raw_back:
1. The disturbance sequences $\{w(t)\}$ and $\{v(t)\}$ are **white and small**.
2. The **nominal trajectory** $x^*(t)$ corresponds to the **disturbance-free** ($w(t) \equiv 0, v(t) \equiv 0$) behavior of the system driven by the nominal input sequence $u^*(t)$, i.e., $x^*(t+1) = f(x^*(t), u^*(t))$.
cards.anki_front: What two assumptions are made on the disturbances \(\{w(t)\} \) and \(\{v(t)\} \) and on the nominal trajectory \((u^*(t), x^*(t))\) when linearizing the nonlinear system (5.8)?
cards.anki_back:
1. The disturbance sequences \(\{w(t)\} \) and \(\{v(t)\} \) are white and small.
2. The nominal trajectory \(x^*(t)\) corresponds to the disturbance-free (\(w(t) \equiv 0, v(t) \equiv 0\)) behavior of the system driven by the nominal input sequence \(u^*(t)\), i.e., \(x^*(t+1) = f(x^*(t), u^*(t))\).

cards.raw_front:
When linearizing the nonlinear system (5.8) around a nominal input $u^*(t)$ and nominal state trajectory $x^*(t)$, how are the perturbation variables $\Delta x(t)$, $\Delta y(t)$, and $\Delta u(t)$ defined?
$$\Delta x(t) = {{c1::x(t) - x^*(t)}}$$
$$\Delta y(t) = {{c1::y(t) - h(x^*(t))}}$$
$$\Delta u(t) = {{c1::u(t) - u^*(t)}}$$
cards.raw_back: Note that $\Delta y(t)$ is the deviation of $y(t)$ from the nominal disturbance-free output $y^*(t) = h(x^*(t))$.
cards.anki_front:
When linearizing the nonlinear system (5.8) around a nominal input \(u^*(t)\) and nominal state trajectory \(x^*(t)\), how are the perturbation variables \(\Delta x(t)\), \(\Delta y(t)\), and \(\Delta u(t)\) defined?

\(\Delta x(t) =\) {{c1::\(x(t) - x^*(t)\)}}

\(\Delta y(t) =\) {{c1::\(y(t) - h(x^*(t))\)}}

\(\Delta u(t) =\) {{c1::\(u(t) - u^*(t)\)}}
cards.anki_back: Note that \(\Delta y(t)\) is the deviation of \(y(t)\) from the nominal disturbance-free output \(y^*(t) = h(x^*(t))\).

cards.raw_front:
Neglecting higher-order nonlinear and cross-disturbance terms around $(x^*(t), u^*(t))$, the perturbation variables $\Delta x(t), \Delta u(t), \Delta y(t)$ satisfy the **linearized LTV state-space model** of Eq. (5.9):
$$\Delta x(t+1) = {{c1::F(t)\Delta x(t) + G(t)\Delta u(t) + \bar{w}(t)}}$$
$$\Delta y(t) = {{c1::H(t)\Delta x(t) + \bar{v}(t)}}$$

$$F(t) = {{c1::\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x}f(x, u)\right|_{x^*(t), u^*(t)}}}, \quad G(t) = {{c1::\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial u}f(x, u)\right|_{x^*(t), u^*(t)}}}, \quad H(t) = {{c1::\left.\frac{\partial}{\partial x}h(x)\right|_{x^*(t)}}}$$

cards.raw_front: When linearizing $x(t+1) = f(x(t), u(t)) + r(x(t), u(t))w(t)$ and $y(t) = h(x(t)) + m(x(t), u(t))v(t)$ into Eq. (5.9), why do derivatives of $r(x,u)$ and $m(x,u)$ not appear in $F(t), G(t), H(t)$?
cards.raw_back:
Expanding $r(x(t), u(t))w(t)$ and $m(x(t), u(t))v(t)$ around $(x^*(t), u^*(t))$ produces **second-order cross terms** between the small state/input perturbations and the small disturbances (such as $\Delta x \cdot w$ and $\Delta x \cdot v$).

Under the **small-disturbance assumption**, both $\Delta x$ and $w, v$ are first-order small quantities, so their products ($\Delta x \cdot w$, $\Delta x \cdot v$) are second-order small and are neglected, leaving $\bar{w}(t) = r(x^*(t), u^*(t))w(t)$ and $\bar{v}(t) = m(x^*(t), u^*(t))v(t)$.

In the linearized LTV model (5.9), the effective process noise $\bar{w}(t) = r(x^*(t), u^*(t))w(t)$ has time-varying covariance matrix $R_1(t)$ given in Eq. (5.10a) by:
$$R_1(t) = E\bar{w}(t)\bar{w}^T(t) = {{c1::r(x^*(t), u^*(t))\,Ew(t)w^T(t)\,r^T(x^*(t), u^*(t))}}$$
cards.raw_back: Even if the underlying white noise $w(t)$ is stationary with constant covariance, $R_1(t)$ becomes time-varying because $r(x^*(t), u^*(t))$ varies along the nominal trajectory.

cards.raw_front: Why is inferring a general nonlinear state-space model from finite data records fundamentally much more demanding than inferring a linear model of the same state dimension?
cards.raw_back:
Even a **first-order deterministic model** ($\dim x = 1$) without disturbances:
$$x(t+1) = f(x(t), u(t)), \quad y(t) = h(x(t))$$
is specified only up to members in an **infinite-dimensional function space** (the unknown functions $f(\cdot,\cdot)$ and $h(\cdot)$), whereas the corresponding first-order linear model is completely characterized by just **two real numbers** (after state-coordinate normalization).

Identify the top and bottom block diagrams in Figure 5.1 and write the intermediate and output signal equations for each.

cards.raw_front: What are the two main ways to parameterize the static nonlinear function $f(\cdot, \eta)$ in a Hammerstein or Wiener model?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Physical parameterization**: Parameterizing $f(\cdot, \eta)$ directly in terms of physical constants, such as saturation breakpoints and saturation levels.
2. **Black-box basis expansion**: Parameterizing $f(\cdot, \eta)$ via flexible basis functions, such as spline-function coefficients or polynomial expansions $f(u) = \sum_{k=1}^m \alpha_k u^k$.

cards.raw_front: Notation & Concept Trap: In the linear regression predictor $\hat{y}(t|\theta) = \varphi^T(t)\theta$ (Eq. 5.12), does the word **"linear"** require the regressor vector $\varphi(t)$ to be a linear function of past inputs $u^t$ and outputs $y^{t-1}$?
cards.raw_back:
**No.** "Linear" in *linear regression* refers strictly to the predictor being **linear in the unknown parameter vector $\theta$**.

It is completely immaterial how $\varphi(t)$ is formed from the data—it can contain arbitrary **nonlinear transformations** $\varphi_i(u^t, y^{t-1})$, provided only that $\varphi(t)$ is a **known (computable) quantity at time $t$** that does not depend on $\theta$.

cards.raw_front:
Why does allowing each input power $u^k(t)$ to have its own independent numerator polynomial $B_k(q)$ in
$$A(q)y(t) = B_1(q)u(t) + B_2(q)u^2(t) + \dots + B_m(q)u^m(t)$$
simplify parameter estimation compared to enforcing $B_k(q) = \alpha_k B(q)$?
cards.raw_back: In a strict Hammerstein cascade $A(q)y(t) = B(q)\sum_{k=1}^m \alpha_k u^k(t)$, the predictor depends on products $\alpha_k b_j$ (bilinear in $\alpha$ and $B$). cards.raw_front:
In **Example 5.1 (A Solar-Heated House)**, why is the ad-hoc linear ARX model (Eq. 5.16)
$$y(t) + a_1 y(t-1) + a_2 y(t-2) = b_1 u(t-1) + b_2 u(t-2) + c_1 I(t-1) + c_2 I(t-2)$$
physically unrealistic for modeling storage temperature $y(t)$ from pump velocity $u(t)$ and solar intensity $I(t)$?
cards.raw_back:
Because the physical effects of solar intensity $I(t)$ and pump velocity $u(t)$ are **multiplicative (interactive), not additive**.

Specifically, if the pump is turned off ($u(t) = 0$), no heated fluid is transported from the solar collector to the storage tank, so solar intensity $I(t)$ does not affect the storage temperature $y(t)$ at all—whereas the linear model (5.16) erroneously predicts that $I(t)$ still heats the storage tank when $u(t)=0$.

cards.raw_front: Why is determining the exact optimal probabilistic predictor for the general nonlinear state-space model (Eq. 5.22) fundamentally intractable in general?
cards.raw_back:
Because the formal probabilistic **nonlinear prediction (filtering) problem has no finite-dimensional solution** except in some isolated special cases (such as linear-Gaussian systems).
\nTracking the exact conditional probability density of $x(t)$ given past measurements $Z^{t-1}$ generally requires an infinite-dimensional state (the entire conditional PDF).

cards.raw_front: Since the exact optimal probabilistic predictor for a general nonlinear state-space model (Eq. 5.22) is unrealizable in finite dimensions, what are the two practical routes to constructing a predictor?

1. **Ad hoc approaches** (such as disregarding process noise $w(t)$ altogether to form a deterministic *simulation model*).
2. **Approximations of the unrealizable optimal nonlinear filter** (e.g., Extended Kalman Filtering or approximate nonlinear filtering as in Jazwinski, 1970, or Anderson and Moore, 1979).
\nIn either case, the resulting predictor takes the general input-output mapping form $\hat{y}(t|\theta) = g(t, Z^{t-1}; \theta)$.

cards.raw_front: What is a **nonlinear simulation model** (Eq. 5.25), and why is it given that name?
cards.raw_back:
A **simulation model** is a predictor constructed from the general nonlinear state-space model (5.22) by **disregarding the process noise $w(t)$** (and setting $v(t)=0$ in the output map):
$$x(t+1, \theta) = f(t, x(t, \theta), u(t), 0; \theta)$$
$$\hat{y}(t|\theta) = h(t, x(t, \theta), u(t), 0; \theta)$$\nIt is called a *simulation model* because the predicted output $\hat{y}(t|\theta)$ is generated purely by simulating a noise-free model driven only by the actual measured input sequence $\{u(t)\}$ (with no feedback from past output measurements $y(t)$).

cards.raw_front: Why is a nonlinear **simulation model** (Eq. 5.26) particularly convenient when physical laws are formulated in **continuous time**?
cards.raw_back:
Because once process noise is set to zero ($w(t) = 0$), generating the predictor $\hat{y}(t|\theta)$ only requires **numerically integrating the deterministic ODE**
$$\frac{d}{dt}x(t, \theta) = f(t, x(t, \theta), u(t), 0; \theta)$$\nusing the measured input trajectory $u(t)$, rather than having to analytically discretize a nonlinear ODE or solve a continuous-discrete nonlinear stochastic filtering problem (Fokker-Planck / Kushner-Stratonovich equation).

cards.raw_front: In Example 5.2 (*Delignification* / cellulose cooking for paper pulp), what are the physical meanings of the state $x(t)$ and the three inputs $u_1(t), u_2(t), u_3(t)$?
cards.raw_back:
- $x(t)$: **Lignin concentration** in the wood chips at time $t$
- $u_1(t)$: **Absolute temperature** at time $t$
- $u_2(t)$: **Concentration of hydrogen sulfite ions**, $[\text{HSO}_3^-]$
- $u_3(t)$: **Concentration of hydrogen ions**, $[\text{H}^+]$

cards.anki_back:

cards.raw_front:
In Example 5.2 (*Delignification*), basic chemical kinetics give the continuous-time nonlinear state equation (Eq. 5.27) for lignin concentration $x(t)$:
{{c1::$$\frac{d}{dt}x(t) = -k_1 e^{-E_L / u_1(t)} [x(t)]^m \cdot [u_2(t)]^\alpha \cdot [u_3(t)]^\beta$$}}
cards.raw_back:
Here:
- $u_1(t)$ is absolute temperature ($e^{-E_L/u_1(t)}$ is the Arrhenius temperature dependence),
- $u_2(t) = [\text{HSO}_3^-]$ and $u_3(t) = [\text{H}^+]$,
- $\theta^T = [E_L, k_1, m, \alpha, \beta]$ is the unknown parameter vector.
cards.anki_front:
In Example 5.2 (Delignification), basic chemical kinetics give the continuous-time nonlinear state equation (Eq. 5.27) for lignin concentration \(x(t)\):
{{c1::\[\frac{d}{dt}x(t) = -k_1 e^{-E_L / u_1(t)} [x(t)]^m \cdot [u_2(t)]^\alpha \cdot [u_3(t)]^\beta\]}}
cards.anki_back:
Here:
- \(u_1(t)\) is absolute temperature (\(e^{-E_L/u_1(t)} \) is the Arrhenius temperature dependence),
- \(u_2(t) = [\text{HSO}_3^-]\) and \(u_3(t) = [\text{H}^+]\),
- \(\theta^T = [E_L, k_1, m, \alpha, \beta]\) is the unknown parameter vector.

cards.raw_front: In the delignification reaction rate equation $\frac{d}{dt}x(t) = -k_1 e^{-E_L / u_1(t)} [x(t)]^m \cdot [u_2(t)]^\alpha \cdot [u_3(t)]^\beta$ (Eq. 5.27), the parameter $E_L$ is called the {{c1::Arrhenius constant}} (scaled activation energy), and the unknown parameter vector is {{c1::$\theta^T = [E_L, k_1, m, \alpha, \beta]$}}.
cards.raw_back: $k_1$ is the pre-exponential reaction rate constant, while $m, \alpha, \beta$ are the reaction orders with respect to lignin concentration $x(t)$, bisulfite concentration $u_2(t) = [\text{HSO}_3^-]$, and hydrogen ion concentration $u_3(t) = [\text{H}^+]$.
cards.anki_front: In the delignification reaction rate equation \(\frac{d}{dt}x(t) = -k_1 e^{-E_L / u_1(t)} [x(t)]^m \cdot [u_2(t)]^\alpha \cdot [u_3(t)]^\beta\) (Eq. 5.27), the parameter \(E_L\) is called the {{c1::Arrhenius constant}} (scaled activation energy), and the unknown parameter vector is {{c1::\(\theta^T = [E_L, k_1, m, \alpha, \beta]\)}}.
cards.anki_back: \(k_1\) is the pre-exponential reaction rate constant, while \(m, \alpha, \beta\) are the reaction orders with respect to lignin concentration \(x(t)\), bisulfite concentration \(u_2(t) = [\text{HSO}_3^-]\), and hydrogen ion concentration \(u_3(t) = [\text{H}^+]\).

cards.raw_front: In Example 5.2 (*Delignification*), how is the continuous-time kinetic law (Eq. 5.27) used as a **nonlinear simulation model** to evaluate candidate parameter vectors $\theta = [E_L, k_1, m, \alpha, \beta]^T$?
cards.raw_back:
1. For a given candidate parameter vector $\theta$, Eq. (5.27) is **numerically simulated** forward in time using the measured input trajectories $\{u_i(t), i=1,2,3\}$ to produce a simulated lignin concentration sequence $\{x(t, \theta)\}$.
2. Since the system output is the lignin concentration itself, the predictor is simply
$$\hat{y}(t|\theta) = x(t, \theta)$$
3. These simulated values $\hat{y}(t|\theta)$ are compared directly with the actually measured lignin concentrations $y(t)$ to evaluate the prediction error $\varepsilon(t, \theta) = y(t) - x(t, \theta)$ associated with $\theta$ (Hagberg and Schöön, 1974).

cards.anki_back:
1. For a given candidate parameter vector \(\theta\), Eq. (5.27) is numerically simulated forward in time using the measured input trajectories \(\{u_i(t), i=1,2,3\} \) to produce a simulated lignin concentration sequence \(\{x(t, \theta)\} \).

\[\hat{y}(t|\theta) = x(t, \theta)\]

cards.raw_front: What is a **nonlinear black-box model structure** in system identification?
cards.raw_back: A flexible parameterization of the general predictor mapping $\hat{y}(t|\theta) = g(Z^{t-1}, \theta)$ designed when there is **no particular physical insight** into the system's properties, intended to cover "all kinds of reasonable system behavior" (the nonlinear counterpart of the linear black-box families in Section 4.2).

cards.anki_back: A flexible parameterization of the general predictor mapping \(\hat{y}(t|\theta) = g(Z^{t-1}, \theta)\) designed when there is no particular physical insight into the system's properties, intended to cover "all kinds of reasonable system behavior" (the nonlinear counterpart of the linear black-box families in Section 4.2).

cards.raw_front: In a time-invariant nonlinear black-box model (omitting explicit time dependence), the general predictor mapping from past data $Z^{t-1}$ to the output space is written as (5.28): {{c1::$$\hat{y}(t|\theta) = g(Z^{t-1}, \theta)$$}}
cards.raw_back: Because $Z^{t-1}$ has a dimension that grows with time $t$, $g(Z^{t-1}, \theta)$ is further decomposed into a regressor mapping $\varphi(t)$ and a static nonlinear function $g(\varphi(t), \theta)$.

cards.anki_back: Because \(Z^{t-1} \) has a dimension that grows with time \(t\), \(g(Z^{t-1}, \theta)\) is further decomposed into a regressor mapping \(\varphi(t)\) and a static nonlinear function \(g(\varphi(t), \theta)\).

cards.raw_front: To handle the increasing number of past observations $Z^{t-1}$, the nonlinear black-box mapping $g(Z^{t-1}, \theta)$ is decomposed as a concatenation of two mappings (5.29)–(5.30): {{c1::$$g(Z^{t-1}, \theta) = g(\varphi(t), \theta), \quad \text{where } \varphi(t) = \varphi(Z^{t-1})$$}}
cards.raw_back: First, $Z^{t-1}$ is mapped into a **finite-dimensional regression vector** $\varphi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ of fixed dimension $d$; second, $g(\varphi, \theta)$ maps $\varphi(t)$ to the space of outputs $\mathbb{R}^p$.

cards.raw_front:
When the formation of the regression vector $\varphi(t)$ from past data $Z^{t-1}$ itself depends on the model parameters $\theta$ (as in NOE, NARMAX, or NBJ models), how is the regressor written (5.31)?
{{c1::$$\varphi(t) = \varphi(Z^{t-1}, \theta) \quad (\text{or for short } \varphi(t, \theta))$$}}
cards.raw_back: This occurs whenever past simulated outputs $\hat{y}(t-k|\theta)$ or past prediction errors $\varepsilon(t-k, \theta)$ are included among the regressors.

When the formation of the regression vector \(\varphi(t)\) from past data \(Z^{t-1} \) itself depends on the model parameters \(\theta\) (as in NOE, NARMAX, or NBJ models), how is the regressor written (5.31)?
{{c1::\[\varphi(t) = \varphi(Z^{t-1}, \theta) \quad (\text{or for short } \varphi(t, \theta))\]}}
cards.anki_back: This occurs whenever past simulated outputs \(\hat{y}(t-k|\theta)\) or past prediction errors \(\varepsilon(t-k, \theta)\) are included among the regressors.

cards.raw_front: Into what **two partial problems** does the concatenation $\hat{y}(t|\theta) = g(\varphi(t), \theta)$ decompose the design of a nonlinear black-box model for dynamical systems?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Regressor selection (dynamics)**: How to choose the finite-dimensional regression vector $\varphi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$ from past inputs and outputs $Z^{t-1}$.
2. **Static function approximation (nonlinearity)**: How to choose the parameterized nonlinear mapping $g(\varphi, \theta)$ from the regressor space $\mathbb{R}^d$ to the output space $\mathbb{R}^p$.
cards.anki_front: Into what two partial problems does the concatenation \(\hat{y}(t|\theta) = g(\varphi(t), \theta)\) decompose the design of a nonlinear black-box model for dynamical systems?
cards.anki_back:
1. Regressor selection (dynamics): How to choose the finite-dimensional regression vector \(\varphi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d\) from past inputs and outputs \(Z^{t-1} \).
2. Static function approximation (nonlinearity): How to choose the parameterized nonlinear mapping \(g(\varphi, \theta)\) from the regressor space \(\mathbb{R}^d\) to the output space \(\mathbb{R}^p\).

cards.raw_front: What do the acronyms **NFIR**, **NARX**, **NOE**, **NARMAX**, and **NBJ** stand for in nonlinear black-box identification, and how are their regressors $\varphi(t)$ defined?
cards.raw_back:
They are the nonlinear counterparts of the linear black-box structures in Table 4.1, classified by which signals appear in $\varphi(t)$:
- **NFIR** (Nonlinear FIR): only past inputs $u(t-k)$.
- **NARX** (Nonlinear ARX): past inputs $u(t-k)$ and measured outputs $y(t-k)$.
- **NOE** (Nonlinear Output Error): past inputs $u(t-k)$ and simulated model outputs $\hat{y}_u(t-k|\theta)$.
- **NARMAX** (Nonlinear ARMAX): $u(t-k)$, $y(t-k)$, and prediction errors $\varepsilon(t-k, \theta)$.
- **NBJ** (Nonlinear Box-Jenkins): full parameterization using $u$, $y$, $\hat{y}_u$, and $\varepsilon$.
cards.anki_front: What do the acronyms NFIR, NARX, NOE, NARMAX, and NBJ stand for in nonlinear black-box identification, and how are their regressors \(\varphi(t)\) defined?
cards.anki_back:
They are the nonlinear counterparts of the linear black-box structures in Table 4.1, classified by which signals appear in \(\varphi(t)\):
- NFIR (Nonlinear FIR): only past inputs \(u(t-k)\).
- NARX (Nonlinear ARX): past inputs \(u(t-k)\) and measured outputs \(y(t-k)\).
- NOE (Nonlinear Output Error): past inputs \(u(t-k)\) and simulated model outputs \(\hat{y}_u(t-k|\theta)\).
- NARMAX (Nonlinear ARMAX): \(u(t-k)\), \(y(t-k)\), and prediction errors \(\varepsilon(t-k, \theta)\).
- NBJ (Nonlinear Box-Jenkins): full parameterization using \(u\), \(y\), \(\hat{y}_u\), and \(\varepsilon\).

cards.raw_front: Which regressor structures are **most commonly used** in nonlinear black-box identification (and why)?
cards.raw_back: **NFIR** and **NARX**, because their regressors $\varphi(t)$ contain **only measured (not estimated/simulated) quantities** $u(t-k)$ and $y(t-k)$, avoiding recurrent parameter-dependent regressors $\varphi(t, \theta)$ and feedback stability issues during estimation.
cards.anki_front: Which regressor structures are most commonly used in nonlinear black-box identification (and why)?
cards.anki_back: NFIR and NARX, because their regressors \(\varphi(t)\) contain only measured (not estimated/simulated) quantities \(u(t-k)\) and \(y(t-k)\), avoiding recurrent parameter-dependent regressors \(\varphi(t, \theta)\) and feedback stability issues during estimation.

cards.raw_front: In the unified basis function expansion framework for scalar-output nonlinear black-box models ($p = 1$, $\varphi \in \mathbb{R}^d$), the mapping $g(\varphi, \theta)$ is parameterized as (5.32): {{c1::$$g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^{n} \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)$$}}
cards.raw_back: Here $g_k(\varphi)$ are called the **basis functions** and $\alpha_k$ are the linear expansion coefficients (coordinates).

cards.anki_back: Here \(g_k(\varphi)\) are called the basis functions and \(\alpha_k\) are the linear expansion coefficients (coordinates).

cards.raw_front: What are the functions $g_k(\varphi)$ called in the nonlinear black-box expansion $g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)$, and why?
cards.raw_back: They are called **basis functions**, because the role they play in $g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)$ is analogous to that of a basis in a functional vector space.
cards.anki_front: What are the functions \(g_k(\varphi)\) called in the nonlinear black-box expansion \(g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)\), and why?
cards.anki_back: They are called basis functions, because the role they play in \(g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)\) is analogous to that of a basis in a functional vector space.

cards.raw_front: Choosing Taylor/polynomial basis functions {{c1::$g_k(\varphi) = \varphi^k$}} (where for $d > 1$, $\varphi^k$ denotes all products of components $\varphi_j$ whose exponents sum to $k$) yields a **Volterra expansion** (5.33).
cards.raw_back: Volterra expansions are global polynomial expansions in past inputs/outputs and have long been tried in nonlinear system modeling.
cards.anki_front: Choosing Taylor/polynomial basis functions {{c1::\(g_k(\varphi) = \varphi^k\)}} (where for \(d > 1\), \(\varphi^k\) denotes all products of components \(\varphi_j\) whose exponents sum to \(k\)) yields a Volterra expansion (5.33).
cards.anki_back: Volterra expansions are global polynomial expansions in past inputs/outputs and have long been tried in nonlinear system modeling.

cards.raw_front: How is the multi-variable monomial notation $\varphi^k$ in (5.33) interpreted when the regression vector $\varphi \in \mathbb{R}^d$ has dimension $d > 1$, and what is the resulting expansion called?
cards.raw_back: For $d > 1$, $\varphi^k$ represents the collection of all products of the regressor components $\varphi_j$ ($j=1,\dots,d$) whose **summed exponents equal $k$**. The resulting expansion $g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_k \alpha_k \varphi^k$ is called a **Volterra expansion**.

cards.anki_back: For \(d > 1\), \(\varphi^k\) represents the collection of all products of the regressor components \(\varphi_j\) (\(j=1,\dots,d\)) whose summed exponents equal \(k\). The resulting expansion \(g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_k \alpha_k \varphi^k\) is called a Volterra expansion.

cards.raw_front: What are the **three essential structural facts** that connect most modern nonlinear black-box model structures via a "mother basis function"?
cards.raw_back:
1. All basis functions $g_k$ are generated from a single **"mother basis function"** denoted generically by $\kappa(x)$.
2. The mother function $\kappa(x)$ is a function of a **scalar variable** $x \in \mathbb{R}$.
3. Individual basis functions $g_k$ are **dilated (scaled) and translated (shifted)** versions of $\kappa(x)$, parameterized by dilation parameters $\beta_k$ and translation parameters $\gamma_k$.
cards.anki_front: What are the three essential structural facts that connect most modern nonlinear black-box model structures via a "mother basis function"?
cards.anki_back:
1. All basis functions \(g_k\) are generated from a single "mother basis function" denoted generically by \(\kappa(x)\).
2. The mother function \(\kappa(x)\) is a function of a scalar variable \(x \in \mathbb{R} \).
3. Individual basis functions \(g_k\) are dilated (scaled) and translated (shifted) versions of \(\kappa(x)\), parameterized by dilation parameters \(\beta_k\) and translation parameters \(\gamma_k\).

cards.raw_front:
In the scalar regressor case ($d = 1$), how is the $k$-th basis function $g_k(\varphi)$ constructed as a dilated and translated version of the mother basis function $\kappa(x)$ (5.34)?
{{c1::$$g_k(\varphi) = g_k(\varphi, \beta_k, \gamma_k) = \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))$$}}
cards.raw_back: Here $\beta_k$ denotes the **dilation (scale) parameter** and $\gamma_k$ denotes the **translation (location) parameter**.
cards.anki_front:
In the scalar regressor case (\(d = 1\)), how is the \(k\)-th basis function \(g_k(\varphi)\) constructed as a dilated and translated version of the mother basis function \(\kappa(x)\) (5.34)?
{{c1::\[g_k(\varphi) = g_k(\varphi, \beta_k, \gamma_k) = \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))\]}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(\beta_k\) denotes the dilation (scale) parameter and \(\gamma_k\) denotes the translation (location) parameter.

cards.raw_front: In the basis function parameterization $g_k(\varphi, \beta_k, \gamma_k) = \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))$, what are the parameters $\beta_k$ and $\gamma_k$ called, and what is their geometric effect on $\kappa$?
cards.raw_back:
- $\beta_k$: **dilation (or scale) parameters** — control the width/steepness/frequency of the basis function (larger $|\beta_k|$ compresses the support).
- $\gamma_k$: **translation (or location) parameters** — shift the center/position of the basis function in the regressor space.
cards.anki_front: In the basis function parameterization \(g_k(\varphi, \beta_k, \gamma_k) = \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))\), what are the parameters \(\beta_k\) and \(\gamma_k\) called, and what is their geometric effect on \(\kappa\)?
cards.anki_back:
- \(\beta_k\): dilation (or scale) parameters — control the width/steepness/frequency of the basis function (larger \(|\beta_k|\) compresses the support).
- \(\gamma_k\): translation (or location) parameters — shift the center/position of the basis function in the regressor space.

cards.raw_front: How is a **Fourier series expansion** represented as a special case of the scalar mother basis function expansion $g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))$?
cards.raw_back:
Take the mother basis function $\kappa(x) = \cos(x)$. Then:
- The dilation parameters $\beta_k$ represent the **frequencies**.
- The translation parameters $\gamma_k$ (via $-\beta_k \gamma_k$) represent the **phases**.
cards.anki_front: How is a Fourier series expansion represented as a special case of the scalar mother basis function expansion \(g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))\)?
cards.anki_back:
Take the mother basis function \(\kappa(x) = \cos(x)\). Then:
- The dilation parameters \(\beta_k\) represent the frequencies.
- The translation parameters \(\gamma_k\) (via \(-\beta_k \gamma_k\)) represent the phases.

cards.raw_front: For piecewise-constant function approximation, the **unit interval indicator** mother basis function $\kappa(x)$ is defined as (5.35): {{c1::$$\kappa(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } 0 \le x < 1 \\ 0 & \text{else} \end{cases}$$}}
cards.raw_back: Choosing $\gamma_k = k\Delta$, $\beta_k = 1/\Delta$, and $\alpha_k = f(k\Delta)$ gives a piecewise-constant approximation of $f$ over intervals $[k\Delta, (k+1)\Delta)$ of length $\Delta$.
cards.anki_front: For piecewise-constant function approximation, the unit interval indicator mother basis function \(\kappa(x)\) is defined as (5.35): {{c1::\[\kappa(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } 0 \le x < 1 \\ 0 & \text{else} \end{cases} \]}}
cards.anki_back: Choosing \(\gamma_k = k\Delta\), \(\beta_k = 1/\Delta\), and \(\alpha_k = f(k\Delta)\) gives a piecewise-constant approximation of \(f\) over intervals \([k\Delta, (k+1)\Delta)\) of length \(\Delta\).

cards.raw_front:
Using the unit interval indicator function $\kappa(x) = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1)}(x)$ in $g(\varphi) = \sum_k \alpha_k \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))$, what parameter choices yield a piecewise-constant approximation of $f(\varphi)$ over a uniform grid of step size $\Delta$?
{{c1::$$\gamma_k = k\Delta, \quad \beta_k = \frac{1}{\Delta}, \quad \alpha_k = f(k\Delta)$$}}
cards.raw_back: Then $\kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k)) = \kappa((\varphi - k\Delta)/\Delta)$ equals $1$ on $k\Delta \le \varphi < (k+1)\Delta$ and $0$ elsewhere.
cards.anki_front:
Using the unit interval indicator function \(\kappa(x) = \mathbf{1}_{[0,1)}(x)\) in \(g(\varphi) = \sum_k \alpha_k \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))\), what parameter choices yield a piecewise-constant approximation of \(f(\varphi)\) over a uniform grid of step size \(\Delta\)?
{{c1::\[\gamma_k = k\Delta, \quad \beta_k = \frac{1}{\Delta}, \quad \alpha_k = f(k\Delta)\]}}
cards.anki_back: Then \(\kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k)) = \kappa((\varphi - k\Delta)/\Delta)\) equals \(1\) on \(k\Delta \le \varphi < (k+1)\Delta\) and \(0\) elsewhere.

cards.raw_front: A smooth local alternative to the unit interval indicator function is the **Gaussian bell** mother basis function (5.36): {{c1::$$\kappa(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2}$$}}
cards.raw_back: The Gaussian bell is a localized, infinitely differentiable basis function whose significant variation is concentrated near $x = 0$.
cards.anki_front: A smooth local alternative to the unit interval indicator function is the Gaussian bell mother basis function (5.36): {{c1::\[\kappa(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}} e^{-x^2/2} \]}}

cards.raw_front: How does Ljung classify single-variable basis functions into **Local Basis Functions** vs. **Global Basis Functions**, and which examples belong to each class?

- **Global Basis Functions**: Functions that have **significant variation over the whole real axis** (e.g., Fourier series $\cos(x)$ and Volterra polynomial expansions $\varphi^k$).

cards.raw_front: What are the **three standard methods** for constructing multi-variable basis functions $g_k(\varphi)$ ($\varphi \in \mathbb{R}^d, d > 1$) from a single-variable mother basis function $\kappa(x)$?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Tensor product construction**: Product of 1-D functions across all $d$ coordinates, $g_k(\varphi) = \prod_{j=1}^d \kappa(\beta_k^j(\varphi_j - \gamma_k^j))$.
2. **Radial construction**: Function of the norm/distance from a center point $\gamma_k$, $g_k(\varphi) = \kappa(\|\varphi - \gamma_k\|_{\beta_k})$.
3. **Ridge construction**: Function of a 1-D linear projection (distance from a hyperplane), $g_k(\varphi) = \kappa(\beta_k^T \varphi + \gamma_k)$.

- $n$: number of basis functions (terms in the expansion)
- $\delta$: target approximation error ($\delta \ll 1$)
- $d$: dimension of the regression vector $\varphi(t) \in \mathbb{R}^d$
- $s$: smoothness (number of continuous derivatives) of the true function $g_0(\varphi)$.

In a **multi-layer network**, the outputs of the first layer of $n$ basis functions are collected into a hidden regressor vector $\varphi^{(2)}(t) = [\varphi_1^{(2)}(t), \dots, \varphi_n^{(2)}(t)]^T$ with components:
{{c1::$$\varphi_k^{(2)}(t) = g_k(\varphi(t)) = \kappa(\varphi(t), \beta_k, \gamma_k)$$}}
cards.raw_back: Instead of linearly combining $\varphi_k^{(2)}(t)$ directly to form the output, $\varphi^{(2)}(t)$ is treated as a new regressor vector fed into a second layer of basis functions.

cards.raw_front: Feeding the first-layer basis outputs $\varphi^{(2)}(t) = [\kappa(\varphi(t), \beta_1, \gamma_1), \dots, \kappa(\varphi(t), \beta_n, \gamma_n)]^T$ into a second expansion layer yields the **two-hidden-layer network** model (5.47): {{c1::$$g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{\ell} \alpha_\ell^{(2)} \kappa\!\left(\varphi^{(2)}, \beta_\ell^{(2)}, \gamma_\ell^{(2)}\right)$$}}
cards.raw_back:
![[assets/fig_5_4_two_hidden_layer_network.png]]
Here $\theta$ collects all parameters across all layers: $\beta_k, \gamma_k, \alpha_\ell^{(2)}, \beta_\ell^{(2)}, \gamma_\ell^{(2)}$.

cards.raw_front: In neural network terminology for (5.47), why are the intermediate basis function layers $\kappa(\varphi(t), \beta_k, \gamma_k)$ and $\kappa(\varphi^{(2)}, \beta_\ell^{(2)}, \gamma_\ell^{(2)})$ called **hidden layers**?
cards.raw_back: Because their internal node outputs **do not show up explicitly as external input/output signals** in the overall model mapping $g(\varphi, \theta)$ (even though their numerical values are of course available to the user inside the algorithm).
cards.anki_front: In neural network terminology for (5.47), why are the intermediate basis function layers \(\kappa(\varphi(t), \beta_k, \gamma_k)\) and \(\kappa(\varphi^{(2)}, \beta_\ell^{(2)}, \gamma_\ell^{(2)})\) called hidden layers?
cards.anki_back: Because their internal node outputs do not show up explicitly as external input/output signals in the overall model mapping \(g(\varphi, \theta)\) (even though their numerical values are of course available to the user inside the algorithm).

cards.raw_front: How many hidden layers are required **in principle** for a basis function network to approximate any practically reasonable nonlinear system, and why might a second hidden layer still be used (Sontag, 1993)?
cards.raw_back: In principle, **one hidden layer** (the standard single-layer basis expansion (5.43) with sufficiently many basis functions $n$) is **universal and sufficient** to model most practically reasonable systems. However, a **second hidden layer** (Sontag, 1993) can provide a more compact/efficient parameterization for certain nonlinear features (such as local piecewise or discontinuous inverse mappings).

cards.raw_front:
What defines a **recurrent network** in terms of the regressor components $\varphi_k(t)$ used at time $t$?
{{c1::$$\varphi_k(t) = g(\varphi(t-k), \theta)$$}} (or more generally, some $\varphi_j(t)$ is obtained as a value from an **interior node** of the network at a previous time instant).
cards.raw_back:
![[assets/fig_5_4_recurrent_network.png]]
Because the regressors depend on past outputs of the model or its internal nodes, $\varphi(t) = \varphi(t, \theta)$ becomes parameter-dependent.

cards.raw_front: What is the distinction between **input/output based recurrent networks** and **state-space based recurrent networks**?
cards.raw_back:
- **Input/output based recurrent networks**: Only **past outputs from the network's output layer** $g(\varphi(t-k), \theta)$ are fed back as recurrent regressors (analogous to NOE models (4.20)).
- **State-space based recurrent networks**: Signals from **any interior (hidden) node** inside the network are delayed and fed back to the input layer as recurrent regressors.
cards.anki_front: What is the distinction between input/output based recurrent networks and state-space based recurrent networks?
cards.anki_back:
- Input/output based recurrent networks: Only past outputs from the network's output layer \(g(\varphi(t-k), \theta)\) are fed back as recurrent regressors (analogous to NOE models (4.20)).
- State-space based recurrent networks: Signals from any interior (hidden) node inside the network are delayed and fed back to the input layer as recurrent regressors.

cards.raw_front: How do the **estimation theory, asymptotic properties, and basic identification algorithms** for nonlinear black-box models compare to those for standard parameterized linear/grey-box models in Ljung's framework?
cards.raw_back: They are **fundamentally the same**: once the nonlinear black-box predictor $\hat{y}(t|\theta) = g(\varphi(t, \theta), \theta)$ is parameterized by a finite vector $\theta$, the general prediction-error estimation theory, asymptotic convergence/distribution results (Chapters 7–9), and gradient-based search algorithms (Chapter 10) apply directly.

cards.raw_front:
In Figure 5.2 (Feedforward network with two hidden layers), trace the signal flow from the input layer to the output layer and explain the role of the constant input `1` entering each layer.
![[assets/fig_5_4_two_hidden_layer_network.png]]
cards.raw_back:

cards.subdeck: 5.5 Nonlinear Black-Box Models - Neural Networks, Wavelets and Classical Models
cards.raw_front: From a system identification perspective, how are neural networks, wavelets, and classical nonlinear black-box estimators unified under a single mathematical framework?
cards.raw_back:
They are all special cases of the general nonlinear function expansion
$$g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)$$
where the basis functions $g_k(\varphi) = \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi - \gamma_k))$ are generated by parameterizing a specific **mother basis function** $\kappa$ with a specific construction rule (ridge, radial, or tensor-product) and scale/location parameters.

cards.subdeck: 5.5 Nonlinear Black-Box Models - Neural Networks, Wavelets and Classical Models
cards.raw_front: In the function expansion framework, a **one-hidden-layer feedforward sigmoid neural network** is obtained by combining a {{c1::ridge}} basis construction with a {{c1::sigmoid}} mother basis function $\kappa$.
cards.raw_back: Specifically, it combines the linear expansion $g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)$ (Eq. 5.32), the ridge construction $g_k(\varphi) = \kappa(\beta_k^T \varphi - \gamma_k)$ (Eq. 5.42), and the sigmoid mother function $\kappa(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}}$ (Eq. 5.38).
cards.anki_front: In the function expansion framework, a one-hidden-layer feedforward sigmoid neural network is obtained by combining a {{c1::ridge}} basis construction with a {{c1::sigmoid}} mother basis function \(\kappa\).
cards.anki_back: Specifically, it combines the linear expansion \(g(\varphi, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k g_k(\varphi)\) (Eq. 5.32), the ridge construction \(g_k(\varphi) = \kappa(\beta_k^T \varphi - \gamma_k)\) (Eq. 5.42), and the sigmoid mother function \(\kappa(x) = \frac{1}{1+e^{-x}} \) (Eq. 5.38).

cards.subdeck: 5.5 Nonlinear Black-Box Models - Neural Networks, Wavelets and Classical Models
cards.raw_front: Both **wavelet networks** (Zhang & Benveniste, 1992) and **radial basis neural networks** (Poggio & Girosi, 1990) are formed by combining a {{c1::Gaussian bell-type}} mother basis function with the {{c1::radial}} multi-variable construction.
cards.raw_back: They pair the local Gaussian mother function $\kappa(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}}e^{-x^2/2}$ (Eq. 5.36) with the radial quadratic norm construction $g_k(\varphi) = \kappa(\|\varphi - \gamma_k\|_{\beta_k})$ (Eq. 5.40).

- **Ljung's general notation**: Called the **mother basis function** and denoted by $\kappa$.
- **Wavelet literature**: Called the **mother wavelet** and denoted by $\psi$.

cards.raw_front: In a one-dimensional dyadic wavelet decomposition, the basis functions are doubly indexed by scale $j$ and location $k$ using dilation parameter {{c1::$\beta_j = 2^j$}} and translation parameter {{c1::$\gamma_k = 2^{-j}k$}}.
cards.raw_back:
Substituting $\beta_j = 2^j$ and $\gamma_k = 2^{-j}k$ into $\kappa(\beta_j(\varphi - \gamma_k))$ yields the standard dyadic wavelet basis:
$$g_{j,k}(\varphi) = \kappa(2^j\varphi - k)$$

cards.anki_back:

cards.raw_front: In terms of the mother wavelet $\kappa$, the doubly indexed 1D dyadic wavelet basis function $g_{j,k}(\varphi)$ (Eq. 5.48) is given by {{c1::$$g_{j,k}(\varphi) = \kappa(2^j \varphi - k), \quad j, k \text{ positive integers}$$}}.
cards.raw_back: Here $j$ indexes the **scale (resolution)** via dilation $2^j$, and $k$ indexes the **spatial/temporal location** at that resolution.

cards.subdeck: 5.5 Nonlinear Black-Box Models - Neural Networks, Wavelets and Classical Models
cards.raw_front: How does a wavelet decomposition improve upon a simple piece-wise constant approximation (using indicator basis functions) over intervals?
cards.raw_back: Wavelets provide **multi-resolution capabilities**: intervals in the regressor space are multiply covered by local basis functions at different scales (resolutions $2^j$), allowing the model to simultaneously capture coarse global trends and fine local details.

cards.subdeck: 5.5 Nonlinear Black-Box Models - Neural Networks, Wavelets and Classical Models
cards.raw_front: What structural property can be achieved in a wavelet basis by suitably choosing the mother wavelet and using dyadic translation/dilation parameters ($\beta_j = 2^j, \gamma_k = 2^{-j}k$), and why is it computationally advantageous?
cards.raw_back: The wavelet basis can be made **orthonormal**. Orthonormality decouples the basis functions, making it computationally very fast and direct to compute the expansion coordinates $\alpha_{j,k}$ in $g(\varphi) = \sum_{j,k} \alpha_{j,k} g_{j,k}(\varphi)$ via inner products without solving an ill-conditioned system.

cards.raw_front: Multi-variable orthonormal wavelet bases are typically constructed via {{c1::tensor products of scalar wavelet functions}}, which restricts their practical use to low regressor dimensions ({{c1::$d \lesssim 3$}}).
cards.raw_back: Because tensor-product grids grow exponentially with the regressor dimension $d$ (the curse of dimensionality), the computational and storage burden rapidly becomes prohibitive for $d > 3$.

cards.raw_front: In classical nonlinear black-box identification, the **Kernel Estimator** (Nadaraya, 1964; Watson, 1969) takes the functional form (Eq. 5.49): {{c1::$$g(\varphi) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \kappa\left(\left\|\frac{\varphi - \gamma_k}{h}\right\|\right)$$}}.
cards.raw_back: Here $\kappa(\cdot)$ is typically a local bell-shaped kernel function, $\gamma_k$ are fixed anchor/data points in the regression vector space, and $h > 0$ is a single global scale (bandwidth) parameter.

How does the Nadaraya-Watson kernel estimator $g(\varphi) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \kappa\left(\left\|\frac{\varphi - \gamma_k}{h}\right\|\right)$ specialize the general radial basis expansion (5.32), (5.34)?

cards.raw_front: How does the **Nearest Neighbor** approach predict the output for a new query regression vector $\varphi^*$ given past estimation data $Z^N$?
cards.raw_back: It searches the past dataset $Z^N$ to find the recorded regression vector $\varphi(t) = \varphi^\dagger$ that is **closest** to $\varphi^*$, and associates $\varphi^*$ directly with the observed output measurement $y(t)$ corresponding to $\varphi(t) = \varphi^\dagger$.

cards.subdeck: 5.5 Nonlinear Black-Box Models - Neural Networks, Wavelets and Classical Models
cards.raw_front:
How is the **Nearest Neighbor** estimator expressed as a special case of the general basis expansion $g(\varphi^*, \theta) = \sum_{k=1}^n \alpha_k \kappa(\beta_k(\varphi^* - \gamma_k))$?

It uses the {{c1::indicator function}} as the mother basis $\kappa$, expanded radially into tightly packed cells centered at {{c1::$\gamma_k = \varphi(k)$}} with weights {{c1::$\alpha_k = y(k)$}} for all $n = N$ data points.
cards.raw_back: When a query $\varphi^*$ arrives, only the cell $t$ whose center $\gamma_t = \varphi(t)$ is closest to $\varphi^*$ evaluates to $\kappa(\beta_t(\varphi^* - \gamma_t)) = 1$ (all others are $0$), yielding $g(\varphi^*, \theta) = \alpha_t = y(t)$.

cards.raw_back: Because B-splines have compact local support, are computationally very simple to evaluate, and can be made as smooth as desired by choosing the polynomial degree, they are widely used in classical interpolation and nonlinear modeling.

cards.raw_front: What two practical properties make **B-splines** particularly attractive as local basis functions in classic interpolation and nonlinear identification problems?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Computational simplicity**: Being piece-wise polynomials with local support, they are very fast and simple to evaluate.
2. **Controllable smoothness**: By selecting the degree of the polynomial pieces, the connections can be made to have continuous derivatives up to any desired order.

cards.raw_front: What is a **fuzzy model** in system identification, and what motivates its use?
cards.raw_back:
A **fuzzy model** (Zadeh, 1975) is a nonlinear model constructed from verbal and imprecise descriptions (a **fuzzy rule base**) of the relationships between measured system signals.

It is motivated by complex systems where setting up precise physical/mathematical differential equations is difficult, but human operators or engineers possess qualitative verbal insight.

A fuzzy model (Zadeh, 1975) is a nonlinear model constructed from verbal and imprecise descriptions (a fuzzy rule base) of the relationships between measured system signals.

It is motivated by complex systems where setting up precise physical/mathematical differential equations is difficult, but human operators or engineers possess qualitative verbal insight.

cards.raw_front: What is a **neuro-fuzzy model** (Jang and Sun, 1995)?
cards.raw_back: A **neuro-fuzzy model** is a fuzzy rule-based model that contains **adjustable parameters** (such as rule conclusion weights $\alpha_k$ or membership scale/location parameters $\beta, \gamma$) that are tuned or estimated from input-output data.
cards.anki_front: What is a neuro-fuzzy model (Jang and Sun, 1995)?
cards.anki_back: A neuro-fuzzy model is a fuzzy rule-based model that contains adjustable parameters (such as rule conclusion weights \(\alpha_k\) or membership scale/location parameters \(\beta, \gamma\)) that are tuned or estimated from input-output data.

cards.raw_front: What two fundamental steps are required to convert a verbal **fuzzy rule base** (e.g., relating outdoor temperature $\varphi_1$ and heater power $\varphi_2$ to room temperature $y$) into a numerical predictor?
cards.raw_back:
1. **Fuzzification (Quantifying attributes)**: Quantify what verbal attributes like "cold outdoors" or "low power" mean for a specific numerical measurement via **membership functions** $\mu_A(\varphi)$.
2. **Inference and Defuzzification (Combining rules)**: Decide to what degree each rule is applicable for the current regressors and combine their conclusions into a single numerical output $y$.
cards.anki_front: What two fundamental steps are required to convert a verbal fuzzy rule base (e.g., relating outdoor temperature \(\varphi_1\) and heater power \(\varphi_2\) to room temperature \(y\)) into a numerical predictor?
cards.anki_back:
1. Fuzzification (Quantifying attributes): Quantify what verbal attributes like "cold outdoors" or "low power" mean for a specific numerical measurement via membership functions \(\mu_A(\varphi)\).
2. Inference and Defuzzification (Combining rules): Decide to what degree each rule is applicable for the current regressors and combine their conclusions into a single numerical output \(y\).

cards.raw_front: In a fuzzy model, each linguistic attribute $A$ (such as "cold", "nice", or "hot") of a regressor $\varphi$ is viewed as a {{c1::fuzzy set}}, and is quantified by a {{c1::membership function $\mu_A(\varphi)$}} taking values in the interval {{c1::$[0, 1]$}}.
cards.raw_back: The value $\mu_A(\varphi) \in [0, 1]$ describes the "degree of membership" of the numerical reading $\varphi$ in the fuzzy set $A$.
cards.anki_front: In a fuzzy model, each linguistic attribute \(A\) (such as "cold", "nice", or "hot") of a regressor \(\varphi\) is viewed as a {{c1::fuzzy set}}, and is quantified by a {{c1::membership function \(\mu_A(\varphi)\)}} taking values in the interval {{c1::\([0, 1]\)}}.
cards.anki_back: The value \(\mu_A(\varphi) \in [0, 1]\) describes the "degree of membership" of the numerical reading \(\varphi\) in the fuzzy set \(A\).

cards.raw_front:
In fuzzy modeling, the piecewise-linear **"soft step" mother function** $\kappa_1(x)$ (Eq. 5.51) is defined as:
$${{c1::\kappa_1(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } x < -1 \\ 1 - (x + 1)/2 & \text{for } -1 \le x < 1 \\ 0 & \text{for } 1 \le x \end{cases}}}$$
cards.raw_back: $\kappa_1(x)$ transitions linearly from $1$ at $x = -1$ down to $0$ at $x = 1$, serving as the prototype for one-sided boundary attributes like "low" or "cold".
cards.anki_front:
In fuzzy modeling, the piecewise-linear "soft step" mother function \(\kappa_1(x)\) (Eq. 5.51) is defined as:
{{c1::\(\kappa_1(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & \text{for } x < -1 \\ 1 - (x + 1)/2 & \text{for } -1 \le x < 1 \\ 0 & \text{for } 1 \le x \end{cases} \)}}
cards.anki_back: \(\kappa_1(x)\) transitions linearly from \(1\) at \(x = -1\) down to \(0\) at \(x = 1\), serving as the prototype for one-sided boundary attributes like "low" or "cold".

cards.raw_front:
In fuzzy modeling, the piecewise-linear **triangle mother function** $\kappa_2(x)$ (Eq. 5.52) is defined as:
$${{c1::\kappa_2(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } |x| > 1 \\ 1 - |x| & \text{for } |x| \le 1 \end{cases}}}$$
cards.raw_back: $\kappa_2(x)$ has a peak of $1$ at $x = 0$ and support $[-1, 1]$, serving as the prototype for intermediate attributes like "nice" or "medium".
cards.anki_front:
In fuzzy modeling, the piecewise-linear triangle mother function \(\kappa_2(x)\) (Eq. 5.52) is defined as:
{{c1::\(\kappa_2(x) = \begin{cases} 0 & \text{for } |x| > 1 \\ 1 - |x| & \text{for } |x| \le 1 \end{cases} \)}}
cards.anki_back: \(\kappa_2(x)\) has a peak of \(1\) at \(x = 0\) and support \([-1, 1]\), serving as the prototype for intermediate attributes like "nice" or "medium".

cards.raw_front:
Using a mother function $\kappa_i(x)$ ($i \in \{1, 2\}$), a fuzzy membership function $\mu_A(\varphi)$ with arbitrary step/peak position and width is parameterized via scale $\beta$ and location $\gamma$ (Eq. 5.53) as:
$${{c1::\mu_A(\varphi) = \kappa_i(\beta(\varphi - \gamma))}}$$
cards.raw_back: Here $\gamma$ centers the transition/peak in regressor coordinates, and $\beta$ controls the steepness (inverse half-width $1/|\beta|$); a negative $\beta$ in $\kappa_1$ flips a falling soft step into a rising soft step.
cards.anki_front:
Using a mother function \(\kappa_i(x)\) (\(i \in \{1, 2\} \)), a fuzzy membership function \(\mu_A(\varphi)\) with arbitrary step/peak position and width is parameterized via scale \(\beta\) and location \(\gamma\) (Eq. 5.53) as:
{{c1::\(\mu_A(\varphi) = \kappa_i(\beta(\varphi - \gamma))\)}}
cards.anki_back: Here \(\gamma\) centers the transition/peak in regressor coordinates, and \(\beta\) controls the steepness (inverse half-width \(1/|\beta|\)); a negative \(\beta\) in \(\kappa_1\) flips a falling soft step into a rising soft step.

cards.raw_front: How is a rising "soft step" membership function (for an upper-bound attribute like "hot" or "high voltage") constructed from the falling soft-step mother function $\kappa_1(x)$ in Eq. (5.51)?
cards.raw_back:
By choosing a **negative scale (dilation) parameter** $\beta < 0$ in $\mu_A(\varphi) = \kappa_1(\beta(\varphi - \gamma))$.

For example, $\mu_{\text{hot}}(\varphi) = \kappa_1(-0.2(\varphi - 20))$ equals $0$ for $\varphi \le 15$, rises linearly from $0$ to $1$ on $[15, 25]$, and equals $1$ for $\varphi \ge 25$.
cards.anki_front: How is a rising "soft step" membership function (for an upper-bound attribute like "hot" or "high voltage") constructed from the falling soft-step mother function \(\kappa_1(x)\) in Eq. (5.51)?
cards.anki_back:
By choosing a negative scale (dilation) parameter \(\beta < 0\) in \(\mu_A(\varphi) = \kappa_1(\beta(\varphi - \gamma))\).

For example, \(\mu_{\text{hot}}(\varphi) = \kappa_1(-0.2(\varphi - 20))\) equals \(0\) for \(\varphi \le 15\), rises linearly from \(0\) to \(1\) on \([15, 25]\), and equals \(1\) for \(\varphi \ge 25\).

cards.raw_front:
A collection of fuzzy sets $A_1, \dots, A_r$ and membership functions for a variable $\varphi$ is called a {{c1::**strong fuzzy partition**}} if it satisfies Eq. (5.54):
$$\sum_{i=1}^r \mu_{A_i}(\varphi) = 1, \quad \forall \varphi$$
cards.raw_back:
![[assets/fig_5_6_membership_functions_temperature.png]]
At every possible value of $\varphi$, the degrees of membership across all $r$ attributes of that variable sum identically to $1$.
cards.anki_front:
A collection of fuzzy sets \(A_1, \dots, A_r\) and membership functions for a variable \(\varphi\) is called a {{c1::strong fuzzy partition}} if it satisfies Eq. (5.54):
\[\sum_{i=1}^r \mu_{A_i}(\varphi) = 1, \quad \forall \varphi\]
cards.anki_back: At every possible value of \(\varphi\), the degrees of membership across all \(r\) attributes of that variable sum identically to \(1\).

cards.raw_front:
What mathematical condition (Eq. 5.54) must hold for the $r$ membership functions $\mu_{A_1}(\varphi), \dots, \mu_{A_r}(\varphi)$ of a regressor $\varphi$ to form a **strong fuzzy partition**?
$${{c1::\sum_{i=1}^r \mu_{A_i}(\varphi) = 1, \quad \forall \varphi}}$$
cards.raw_back: This partition-of-unity condition ensures that adjacent membership transitions complement each other exactly at every regressor point $\varphi$.
cards.anki_front:
What mathematical condition (Eq. 5.54) must hold for the \(r\) membership functions \(\mu_{A_1}(\varphi), \dots, \mu_{A_r}(\varphi)\) of a regressor \(\varphi\) to form a strong fuzzy partition?
{{c1::\(\sum_{i=1}^r \mu_{A_i}(\varphi) = 1, \quad \forall \varphi\)}}
cards.anki_back: This partition-of-unity condition ensures that adjacent membership transitions complement each other exactly at every regressor point \(\varphi\).

cards.raw_front:
![[assets/fig_5_6_membership_functions_temperature.png]]
In Figure 5.4, how are the three outdoor temperature membership functions (`cold`, `nice`, and `hot`) parameterized using $\kappa_1$ and $\kappa_2$, and why do they form a **strong fuzzy partition**?
cards.raw_back:
- **Solid (`cold`)**: $\mu_{\text{cold}}(\varphi) = \kappa_1(0.2(\varphi - 10))$, transitioning from $1$ to $0$ over $[5, 15]^\circ\text{C}$.
- **Dashed (`nice`)**: $\mu_{\text{nice}}(\varphi) = \kappa_2(0.1(\varphi - 15))$, triangle peaking at $15^\circ\text{C}$ with support $[5, 25]^\circ\text{C}$.
- **Dotted (`hot`)**: $\mu_{\text{hot}}(\varphi) = \kappa_1(-0.2(\varphi - 20))$, transitioning from $0$ to $1$ over $[15, 25]^\circ\text{C}$.

They form a **strong fuzzy partition** because on every interval ($\varphi < 5$, $[5,15]$, $[15,25]$, $\varphi > 25$), the slopes and values of the active functions sum identically to $1$.

cards.anki_back:
- Solid (cold): \(\mu_{\text{cold}}(\varphi) = \kappa_1(0.2(\varphi - 10))\), transitioning from \(1\) to \(0\) over \([5, 15]^\circ\text{C} \).
